extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, astronomers, and advanced students studying Newton's Principia and classical geometric constructions
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures, lemmas and propositions for constructing curves (conic sections, trajectories, trapezia, triangles) and for locating bodies on given orbits (parabola, ellipse) using classical geometric methods and transformations. Includes formal geometric facts used as construction rules and practical approximation procedures for orbital position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of tangency and analytic order under coordinate scaling
rubrics_metrics.description: If a point G is tangent to a straight line (or to a conic or any analytic curve of given order) in the original figure, then the corresponding transformed point g (after changing abscissas and ordinates by specified proportional factors) is tangent to the corresponding straight line (or conic or analytic curve) in the new figure; likewise the analytic order of the curve is preserved under the transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton shows that replacing AD and DG by OA×AB÷ad and OA×dg÷ad (i.e., performing a proportional substitution of abscissae/ordinates) produces a new equation whose indeterminates have the same number of dimensions, so tangency and analytic order are preserved. Use this when mapping problems to transformed figures: tangency relations and curve order remain invariant under these axis-scaling/affine-like substitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation/transfer of tangents and defining elements between figures
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line is tangent to a given curved line in the first figure, the translated line will be tangent to the corresponding curved line in the transformed figure, and conversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To transform a curved figure, transfer its defining points, tangents, and other lines; tangents map to tangents under the translation/transform. This is the practical rule for performing the inverse transformation after solving the problem in the simpler (transformed) figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce complex figures by transferring intersections or defining elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To transform a rectilinear figure into another, it suffices to transfer intersections of lines and draw corresponding lines in the new figure; to transform a curvilinear figure, transfer its points of contact, tangents, and other straight lines that define the curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this lemma to simplify difficult problems by transforming figures so that converging lines become parallel (choosing an appropriate line as the first ordinate). After solving in the transformed figure, revert via inverse operations to obtain the solution in the original figure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of transformations to convert converging lines into parallels
rubrics_metrics.description: By choosing for the primary ordinate any straight line that passes through the concurrence of converging lines, one may transform any system of convergent lines into a system of parallel lines (concurrent point sent to infinity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique simplifies constructions: solve the problem where tangents become parallel (easier case), then apply the inverse transformation. Emphasized as useful for solving more difficult planar and solid problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXIII — locating a point K under given ratio constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: If two given position lines AC, BD terminate at given points A, B and have a given ratio to one another, and the line CD joining indeterminate points C, D is cut in a given ratio at K, then the point K is located on a given position line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: let AC and BD meet at E; on BE take BG such that AE:BG = BD:AC; set FD = EG etc., complete parallelogram ELKH to locate K on the given position side HK. Use when a point must be placed so that a division ratio on a joining line yields a point constrained to a fixed line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXIV — semidiameter as mean proportional for conic tangents
rubrics_metrics.description: If two parallel tangents AF and GB touch a conic section and a third tangent EF meets them in F and G, then the semidiameter CD parallel to the two tangents is the mean proportional between the segments (from contact points) intercepted by the two parallel tangents and the third tangent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal relation given: AF, CD, BG are in continuous proportion. Corollaries derive further proportional relations among segments and show concurrency properties of lines through contact points and the centre. Use for computations and locating contact points when two tangents are parallel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXV — proportions of abscissas for parallelogram tangents to a conic
rubrics_metrics.description: If the four sides of a parallelogram tangent to any conic are infinitely produced and cut by any fifth tangent, and abscissas are taken terminating at opposite angles of the parallelogram, then the abscissa of one side to that side is as the adjacent part of the neighbouring side between the contact point and the third side is to the abscissa of that neighbouring side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit proportional equalities (e.g., ME:MI = BK:KQ and KH:KL = AM:MF) and corollaries equating rectangles constructed from these segments. Use when handling tangents intersecting parallelograms and relating segments algebraically in constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXV (Prob. XVII) — construct a trajectory through two given points and tangent to three given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: To describe a curve that passes through two given points and is tangent to three given position lines: translate the tangent lines so that, in the transformed figure (using Lemma), two of them become parallel and the third becomes parallel to the line through the two given points; find the three contact points in the transformed figure and transfer them back to the original by the inverse operation to obtain the required trajectory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: use the concurrency-of-tangents construction to make two tangents parallel; identify contact points c,d,e via proportional constructions; inverse-transfer yields contact points on original figure, then apply Problem XIV to describe the trajectory. Note impossibility cases when one of the given points lies between certain contact points (problem becomes impossible).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVI (Prob. XVIII) — construct a trajectory through a given point and tangent to four given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: From the common intersection of two tangents and the common intersection of the remaining two, draw a line which, transformed as primary ordinate, makes pairs of tangents parallel; in the transformed figure two contact points P and its conjugate q are found which transfer back to two points in the original figure defining the trajectory (then use Prop. XVII).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to Prop. XVII by an appropriate affine-like transformation (Lemma XXII). The constructed pair of points in the original figure yields the required trajectory via the method of the previous problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXVI — place a triangle of given shape and size with angles tangent to three given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three position lines (not all parallel), construct a triangle of given shape and magnitude so that each vertex angle is tangent to the corresponding given line (i.e., locate triangle DEF so D-angle touches AB, E-angle touches AC, F-angle touches BC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: describe circular segments on the triangle sides equal to the given vertex angles, complete them to circles, find intersections and centers P,Q, use similarity and proportional arcs to position a triangle equal and similar to ABC. Corollary: reduces to constructing a straight line composed of given parts between three given position lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXVIII & XXIX (Probs. XX & XXIX) — construct trajectories similar to a given curve whose parts are intercepted by given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a curve DEF and three (or four) position lines that cut it, construct a trajectory similar and equal to DEF such that its parts are cut by the given lines in the same proportions and order as the original. The method reduces to placing a triangle/trapezium with specified tangency (Lemmata XXVI/XXVII) and then describing a similar curve about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General recipe: construct the polygonal frame (triangle/trapezium) with prescribed angle/tangency properties (via the corresponding lemma), then draw a curve similar & equal to the given one relative to that frame. Scholium gives alternate constructions and proportional constructions for the same problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXVII — construct a trapezium with angles tangent to four given lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Given four position lines (not all parallel nor concurrent), construct a trapezium similar to a given trapezium FGHI whose angles f,g,h,i are tangent respectively to the four given lines. The lemma provides a circle-and-proportion construction to locate points a,b,c completing a figure similar to the given one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use circles whose arcs subtend angles equal to the given contact angles, take centers and proportional segments on the line joining centers, then complete the similar figure. Corollary: used to produce straight lines composed of parts that sit between four given lines with given proportional lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXVIII — impossibility of finite-term algebraic expression for oval area and related lengths
rubrics_metrics.description: No oval figure exists whose area (measured by abscissas laid off by straight lines at will) can in general be found by finite algebraic equations (finite number of terms/dimensions). Consequently, intersections with spirals or infinite-root equations show infinite many roots, so such areas/lengths are not generally expressible by finite algebraic formulae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton argues via the spiral generated by revolving a radius with point moving proportional to arc length: intersections with a straight line are infinite, requiring infinitely many roots/dimensions, contradicting finite algebraic equations. Corollary: area of an ellipse as function of time is not expressible by a finite algebraic equation; distinguishes 'geometrice rationales' (algebraically integrable) from 'geometrice irrationales' (e.g., spirals, quadratrix, trochoids). Use this to justify necessity of iterative/approximate methods for orbital problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXX (Prob. XXII) — locate a body on a given parabolic trajectory at a given time
rubrics_metrics.description: For a body moving in a given parabola with umbilicus S and principal vertex A, the area APS described by the radius SP from the umbilicus is proportional to time; by bisecting AS at G and erecting perpendicular GH equal to 3M (M a constructed measure proportional to time), the circle centered at H with radius HS meets the parabola at the required location P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: compute a length GH = 3M (where 4·AS·M equals the parabolic area APS), draw circle center H radius HS; intersection with parabola yields P. Corollaries give velocity ratios (e.g., speed at H vs speed at A is 3:8) and show how to inverse the construction to find time for a given arc by erecting GH over the midpoint of AS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XXXI (Prob. XXIII) — locate a body on a given elliptical trajectory at a given time (geometric and practical algorithms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an ellipse (A vertex, S umbilicus, O centre), Newton gives a geometric construction and practical approximations to find the body's position P at a specified time using the proportionality of swept area to time: transform using circumscribed circles and trochoid construction (or use approximate series methods based on mean motion and corrective angles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exact geometric recipe: extend OA to G with OG:OA = OA:OS, erect GH and describe circle center O radius OG, roll the circle to generate a trochoid; choose GK proportional to elapsed-time/period to find L on trochoid, then draw LP to meet ellipse at P. Scholium: practical astronomers use approximations — compute mean anomaly (angle proportional to time), then correction angles (equations of center) V, X found by trigonometric relations (series expansion), iterating to rapidly convergent series ACQ + E + G + I ...; alternative construction approximations and procedures for hyperbola and near-apsidal cases are provided. The method relies on area APS equalling difference between arc and chord-type rectilinear quantities; Newton also provides specific small-angle series guidance and notes on convergence and typical accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction principle — solve by transforming to previously solved cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the propositions reduce novel construction problems to earlier solved problems by transforming the figure (making tangents parallel, mapping to trapezia/triangles) so that one can apply prior constructions and then inverse-transform back to original configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a meta-rule repeated throughout: when faced with a new construction (trajectory with given tangents/points), seek a transformation sending the problem to a case with parallel tangents or previously treated polygonal frame; after solving in transformed domain, apply inverse mapping. Watch for impossibility cases noted in the text (e.g., special positions of points yielding no solution).
